hits.draft_en:
Getting frontend CI below 2 minutes is not magic, it is five boring decisions stacked together:

- bun check replaces tsc
- oxlint with as many rules switched on as possible
- shard sizes balanced by how long each test really took before
- pull requests skip any test their diff cannot touch
- every stage (lint, typecheck, build, tests) kicks off at once instead of waiting in line

hits.name: kaize
hits.text:
All code is slop, except mine

That’s what Lauren Tan, the engineer behind Grok Bot, said on stage

She ships 3,000+ pull requests a month, and her secret is what she does every time an agent makes a mistake

Most people just add another line to AGENTS.md

Lauren runs every mistake through 4 questions instead:

> Can I redesign the code so this mistake is impossible?
> Can a lint rule or a type catch it automatically?
> Can the agent catch it by running and checking its own work?
> Does it really need a written rule?

Each mistake gets one of 5 fixes:

Redesign / lint / verify / write a rule / human review

The useful part is that a written rule is only one option, not the default

Most of her fixes never touch AGENTS.md at all

> Sometimes the answer is to ban something entirely, like useEffect
> Sometimes it’s a lint rule: her team went from 7 to 167 of them in four months
> Sometimes it’s letting the agent prove its work with screenshots

Mistake -> cheapest permanent fix -> never catch it by hand again

Lauren’s all rules:

Wild times.

hits.name: Avi Chawla
hits.text:
Coding agent just got a lot more independent:

They can now do the one thing they used to need you for.

When you ask an agent to build an app, it can write the schema, the routes, and the data layer in a few minutes.

But then it needs a database, and everything stops since someone has to open a browser, create an account, provision a database, set up a user, and paste the connection string back into the session.

Those steps were built for a human, so the agent just waits for you to complete them.

MongoDB just solved that with Atlas Ephemeral Clusters.

Now, your agent can make one API call, and Atlas returns a live database in under a minute.

Your agent saves the connection string, allowing you to keep building on a real MongoDB Atlas cluster.

You can learn more here: https://t.co/1AvhBezHTV

The part I like most is that the agent can create the database cluster and work with the data, but only a human can make the decision to claim it and take ownership.

If you don’t claim it, the cluster pauses after 48 hours and deletes itself after 7 days, so abandoned experiments clean themselves up automatically.

If you claim it, it becomes a permanent free Atlas cluster with the same data and the same connection string.

So the agent handles the setup end-to-end, and you only step in once the project is worth keeping.

Atlas Ephemeral Clusters are in public preview, and the docs shared above walk you through the full flow.

The video below shows this in action, and I worked with the MongoDB team to put this together.

If you are building with coding agents, the next step is getting several of them to work together on one project.

I wrote a full breakdown of how Claude Code handles that with subagents and agent teams.

It covers when a subagent is enough, when you need a team of agents that coordinate with each other, and how each setup manages context and hands off work.

Read it below.

virals.name: Tech with Mak
virals.text:
Researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences cut AI-agent token consumption by up to 92.9%, without retraining a single model.

They also reduced execution time by up to 89%.

The problem is familiar if you've built AI agents. Ask a coding agent to investigate one error, and it may read an entire log, repository file, or document when only a few passages are relevant.

Those unnecessary tokens can remain in context across subsequent model calls, increasing cost and latency.

The researchers developed SparseRead, a system that controls what an agent reads before the content enters the model's context.

It works through three components →

1./ Read Intent Protocol: Tracks what information the agent needs, which evidence has been found, and what remains unresolved.

2./ Adaptive Reader Backends: Locate relevant evidence across documents, PDFs, code repositories, and structured data.

3./ Budgeted Read Gate: Limits how much source content enters context, with the option to fall back to reading the complete file.

Across six models and five workload scenarios, the researchers reported →
> Up to 92.9% fewer tokens consumed.
> Up to 89% less execution time.
> Median reductions of 61.4% in tokens and 53.7% in time.
> Task quality preserved or improved in most evaluated settings.

No model retraining is required.

The interesting engineering lesson is that context optimization doesn't have to begin with compression or KV caching.

You can reduce a substantial amount of work by controlling what enters the context in the first place.

(Link to the paper and code in comments)

outsiders.name: Tech with Mak
outsiders.text:
Researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences cut AI-agent token consumption by up to 92.9%, without retraining a single model.

They also reduced execution time by up to 89%.

The problem is familiar if you've built AI agents. Ask a coding agent to investigate one error, and it may read an entire log, repository file, or document when only a few passages are relevant.

Those unnecessary tokens can remain in context across subsequent model calls, increasing cost and latency.

The researchers developed SparseRead, a system that controls what an agent reads before the content enters the model's context.

It works through three components →

1./ Read Intent Protocol: Tracks what information the agent needs, which evidence has been found, and what remains unresolved.

2./ Adaptive Reader Backends: Locate relevant evidence across documents, PDFs, code repositories, and structured data.

3./ Budgeted Read Gate: Limits how much source content enters context, with the option to fall back to reading the complete file.

Across six models and five workload scenarios, the researchers reported →
> Up to 92.9% fewer tokens consumed.
> Up to 89% less execution time.
> Median reductions of 61.4% in tokens and 53.7% in time.
> Task quality preserved or improved in most evaluated settings.

No model retraining is required.

The interesting engineering lesson is that context optimization doesn't have to begin with compression or KV caching.

You can reduce a substantial amount of work by controlling what enters the context in the first place.

(Link to the paper and code in comments)
